target: Me pone un cortado, por favor

cortado.en-GB: espresso with a dash of milk

mnemonic.title: Cortado: a cut coffee
mnemonic.text: «Cortado» is espresso “cut” (cortar) with a dash of milk: picture a knife through a black coffee.

grammar.title: «Me pone…»
grammar.text: «Me pone…» (literally “will you put me…”) is the everyday way to order in Spain. It is the usted form of poner, but it doesn't sound stiff.

pronunciation.title: Soft d, ng before c
pronunciation.respelling: meh POH-neh oong kor-TAH-doh, por fah-VOR
pronunciation.text: The d in cortado is soft, close to the th in “this”. The n of un sounds like ng before the c.

mnemonic.title: Oats in the oven
mnemonic.text: «Avena» sounds a little like “oven”: picture a tray of oats baking in one. «Leche de avena» is oat milk.

grammar.title: Asking the whole café
grammar.text: «Tienen» speaks to the whole place (ustedes). It's the natural way to ask what a café has.

pronunciation.title: A soft v
pronunciation.text: The v in avena is a soft b: the lips come close but don't touch.

mnemonic.title: The bill counts
mnemonic.text: «Cuenta» comes from «contar», to count: the bill counts up what you had.

grammar.title: Always «la cuenta»
grammar.text: Say «la cuenta», with “the”: it's the bill for this table, so never «una cuenta».

pronunciation.title: The “kw” in cuenta
pronunciation.text: Cue sounds like “kweh”, and the stress falls on it.

translations.en-GB: Can we sit on the terrace?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли да седнем на терасата?

mnemonic.title: Terraza, terrace
mnemonic.text: «Terraza» is the English “terrace”: in Spain it means the tables outside a café.

grammar.title: Where «nos» goes
grammar.text: «Nos» can go before the verb or on the end: «¿Podemos sentarnos…?» means the same.

pronunciation.title: Castilian z and rr
pronunciation.respelling: nos poh-DEH-mos sen-TAR en lah teh-RRAH-thah
pronunciation.text: In Spain the z in terraza sounds like the th in “think”. The rr is rolled.

mnemonic.title: Sin, without
mnemonic.text: «Sin» means “without”; its opposite is «con», with: café con leche, sin gluten.

grammar.title: «Sin» without an article
grammar.text: «Sin» takes no article: sin azúcar, sin lactosa, sin gluten.

pronunciation.title: GLU-ten
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable, with a short, pure u.

mnemonic.title: Recommend, Spanish style
mnemonic.text: «Recomienda» is English “recommend” with a Spanish middle: re-co-MIEN-da. Picture the waiter tapping the best dish on «MIEN».

grammar.title: Polite «recomienda»
grammar.text: «Recomienda» is the usted form, polite with a waiter. With friends: «¿Qué nos recomiendas?».

pronunciation.title: The ie in recomienda
pronunciation.text: The ie is one syllable, “yeh”: re-co-MIEN-da.

target: Una ración de croquetas, por favor

mnemonic.title: A ration of croquettes
mnemonic.text: «Ración» sounds like “ration”: picture a soldier’s ration, except it’s a whole plate of croquettes to share.

grammar.title: «De» joins the food
grammar.text: A dish of something takes «de»: una ración de croquetas, un plato de jamón.

pronunciation.title: Castilian c in ración
pronunciation.respelling: OO-nah rah-THYON deh kro-KEH-tahs, por fah-VOR
pronunciation.text: In Spain the c of ración sounds like the th in “think”, and the r at the start is rolled.

translations.en-GB: Could you bring us another round?
translations.bg-BG: Ще ни донесете ли още по едно?

mnemonic.title: A round is a ronda
mnemonic.text: «Ronda» is a round of drinks, like a lap of a race: one more for the whole table.

grammar.title: «Otra», never «una otra»
grammar.text: «Otra» already means “another”, so it never takes «una».

pronunciation.title: Rolled r in ronda
pronunciation.text: An r at the start of a word is rolled, like rr: «ronda». «Trae» keeps both vowels: TRA-e.

mnemonic.title: Stretch the word
mnemonic.text: Say «buenísimo» with a long, happy «-ísimo»: the longer the ending, the better the food.

grammar.title: «Está» for taste
grammar.text: Use «está» for how food tastes right now. «-ísimo» turns an adjective up: bueno → buenísimo.

pronunciation.title: Stress on -ní-
pronunciation.text: Buenísimo is stressed on «ní», as its accent shows; «bue» is one syllable, “bweh”.

mnemonic.title: Beer through a cane
mnemonic.text: «Caña» is a cane or reed, as in «caña de azúcar», sugar cane: picture sipping a small beer through a hollow cane.

grammar.title: Una: caña is feminine
grammar.text: «Caña» ends in -a and is feminine, so it takes «una», not «un».

pronunciation.title: The ñ
pronunciation.text: ñ sounds like the ny in “canyon”.

mnemonic.title: Station with an e
mnemonic.text: «Estación» is “station” with an e in front: Spanish adds one before s and a consonant, as in «España» and «estudiante».

grammar.title: Estar for where
grammar.text: Where something is takes «estar»: ¿Dónde está…? Use «hay» to ask whether there is one: ¿Hay metro aquí?

pronunciation.title: Stress on -ción
pronunciation.respelling: DON-deh es-TAH lah es-tah-THYON deh MEH-tro
pronunciation.text: Words in -ción are stressed on the end, and the c sounds like th in Spain.

translations.bg-BG: Един билет в едната посока, моля
translations.ru-RU: Один билет в одну сторону, пожалуйста

mnemonic.title: A ticket paid by ticket
mnemonic.text: «Billete» starts like “bill”. In Spain a banknote is also a «billete», so picture paying for your ticket with a ticket.

grammar.title: Adjective after the noun
grammar.text: Most adjectives follow the noun: un billete sencillo. A return is un billete de ida y vuelta.

pronunciation.title: Ll in billete
pronunciation.text: Ll sounds like the y in “yes”, and un before b sounds like “oom”.

translations.en-GB: Does this train go to Sol?
translations.bg-BG: Този влак ходи ли до Сол?

mnemonic.title: Sol, the sun
mnemonic.text: «Sol» means “sun”: Madrid's Puerta del Sol, at the centre of the city, is the Gate of the Sun.

grammar.title: «Ir a» + place
grammar.text: Going somewhere is «ir a»: va a Sol. Sol (Puerta del Sol) is Madrid's central station.

pronunciation.title: A tapped r in tren
pronunciation.text: In «tren» the r is a single quick tap, and before «va» the n sounds like m.

translations.en-GB: Which station do I get off at?

mnemonic.title: Bajo, down
mnemonic.text: «Bajo» is “low”, as in «planta baja», the ground floor: bajarse is to step down off the train.

grammar.title: Bajarse and subirse
grammar.text: «Bajarse» is to get off; «subirse» is to get on.

pronunciation.title: J from the throat
pronunciation.text: The j is a rough h from the back of the throat, like the ch in Scottish “loch”.

translations.en-GB: How much is it per kilo?

mnemonic.title: Cuánto, quantity
mnemonic.text: «Cuánto» shares its root with “quantity”: how much, per kilo.

grammar.title: Today's price
grammar.text: «¿A cuánto está…?» asks for today's price of things whose price changes, like fruit.

pronunciation.title: Kwan in cuánto
pronunciation.text: «Cuán» is one syllable, “kwan”, and it carries the stress.

translations.en-GB: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please

mnemonic.title: Put, as in “postpone”
mnemonic.text: «Póngame» is from «poner», to put, the Latin root of English “postpone” (put after) and “component” (put together): put me half a kilo.

grammar.title: No «un» before medio
grammar.text: «Póngame» is the usted command of poner, normal at a stall. «Medio kilo» takes no «un».

pronunciation.title: Stress on pón-
pronunciation.text: The accent on «pón» keeps the stress there once «me» is added; n before g sounds like ng.

translations.en-GB: Could you wrap it for me?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли да ми го опаковате?

mnemonic.title: Envolver, envelope
mnemonic.text: «Envolver» is to wrap, like an envelope around a letter.

grammar.title: Me before lo
grammar.text: Two pronouns go before the verb in this order: me (for me), then lo (it).

pronunciation.title: Hard and soft v
pronunciation.text: After n the v is a full b, “em-bol”; the second v is soft, the lips barely touch.

mnemonic.title: Más sounds like max
mnemonic.text: «Más» (more) sounds like “max”: you’ve hit your max, so it’s «nada más», nothing more.

grammar.title: Nada más
grammar.text: «Nada más» means “nothing more”. Spanish can stack negatives: «No quiero nada más».

pronunciation.title: Soft d in nada
pronunciation.text: The d of nada is soft, like th in “this”; in Spain gracias has a th sound too.

translations.en-GB: What do you do for a living?

mnemonic.title: Dedicated to
mnemonic.text: «Dedicarse a» is what you are dedicated to: your work.

grammar.title: Tú or usted
grammar.text: «Te» makes this informal (tú). To a stranger, say «¿A qué se dedica?».

pronunciation.title: Soft d in dedicas
pronunciation.text: Both d's of dedicas are soft, between vowels: said lightly, almost a th.

translations.en-GB: We had such a good time!

mnemonic.title: The evening passed well
mnemonic.text: Picture the evening passing well: «pasarlo bien» is to have a good time.

grammar.title: Pasarlo bien
grammar.text: «Pasarlo bien» means to have a good time. Spain often uses «hemos pasado» for something that happened today.

pronunciation.title: A silent h
pronunciation.text: The h of hemos is silent: “eh-MOS”.

mnemonic.title: Ya, right now
mnemonic.text: «Ya» sounds like “yeah”: yeah, I really have to go now.

grammar.title: Tener que
grammar.text: «Tener que» + infinitive means “have to”. «Ya» here means “now, already”.

pronunciation.title: Tengo: ng
pronunciation.text: N before g sounds like ng in “finger”; «que» is just “keh”, the u is silent.

translations.en-GB: Shall we meet up next week?
translations.bg-BG: Да се видим ли следващата седмица?

mnemonic.title: The week that comes
mnemonic.text: «La semana que viene» is, word for word, “the week that comes”: next week.

grammar.title: Quedar
grammar.text: «Quedar» means to arrange to meet. «La semana que viene» is next week.

pronunciation.title: Qu is k
pronunciation.text: Qu sounds like k; in quedamos the d between vowels is soft.

mnemonic.title: Libre, at liberty
mnemonic.text: «Libre» is “free”, as in “liberty”: picture the green light on a Spanish taxi’s roof saying it’s at liberty to take you.

grammar.title: Estar for now
grammar.text: «Está libre» uses «estar»: free right now. «Es libre» would mean free by nature.

pronunciation.title: Br in libre
pronunciation.text: The b in libre is soft, and the r after it is a single tap.

mnemonic.title: Address, direction
mnemonic.text: «Dirección» is “address”, and it looks like “direction”: the address tells the driver which direction to go.

grammar.title: Esta, this
grammar.text: «Esta» (this) matches «dirección», which is feminine; with a masculine noun it is «este»: este hotel.

pronunciation.title: Dirección: two c's
pronunciation.text: The first c is a k, the second a th: dee-rek-THYON.

translations.en-GB: How much do I owe you?

mnemonic.title: Debo, debt
mnemonic.text: «Debo» (I owe) shares its root with “debt”: how much is my debt?

grammar.title: Polite «le»
grammar.text: «Le» is the polite “you”. To a friend: «¿Cuánto te debo?».

pronunciation.title: Soft b in debo
pronunciation.text: Between vowels both the d and the b of debo are soft.

mnemonic.title: Pare, park
mnemonic.text: «Pare» sounds like the start of “park”: stop and park here.

grammar.title: Pare, aquí mismo
grammar.text: «Pare» is the usted command of parar. «Aquí mismo» means right here.

pronunciation.title: Aquí: ah-KEE
pronunciation.text: The u in «aquí» is silent: ah-KEE, stressed on the end.

mnemonic.title: Моля: please
mnemonic.text: «Моля» is both “please” and “you are welcome”, like German «bitte».

grammar.title: Neuter «едно»
grammar.text: «Кафе» is neuter, so “one” is «едно».

pronunciation.title: ka-FE
pronunciation.text: Stress the last syllable of кафе.

mnemonic.title: Сметка counts
mnemonic.text: «Сметка» comes from «смятам», to count: the bill counts up what you had.

grammar.title: “The” is a suffix
grammar.text: Bulgarian adds “the” to the end of the word: сметка (a bill) → сметката (the bill).

pronunciation.title: SMET-ka-ta
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable; the unstressed a's are short and neutral.

mnemonic.title: Без: without
mnemonic.text: «Без» means “without”, as in Russian: мляко без лактоза, кафе без захар.

grammar.title: Questions with «ли»
grammar.text: «Ли» turns a sentence into a yes/no question. It comes right after the word you ask about.

pronunciation.title: A soft л in мляко
pronunciation.text: «Мля» is one syllable with a soft l: “mlya”.

mnemonic.title: Вкус: taste
mnemonic.text: «Вкусно» comes from «вкус», taste: it is full of taste.

grammar.title: «Е» comes second
grammar.text: The short «е» (is) usually comes second in the sentence: много е вкусно.

pronunciation.title: в sounds like f
pronunciation.text: The в at the start of «вкусно» sounds like f before к: “fkoos-no”.

mnemonic.title: Where the bus «спира»
mnemonic.text: A «спирка» is where the bus «спира», stops: hear «спир-» as “stop” in both words.

grammar.title: Къде е…?
grammar.text: «Къде е…?» asks where something is. The same «е» (is) serves every noun: къде е спирката, къде е хотелът.

pronunciation.title: The ъ in къде
pronunciation.text: «Ъ» in къде is short and neutral, and the stress is on «де».

mnemonic.title: Билет: ticket
mnemonic.text: «Билет» is the French «billet» and the Spanish «billete»: a ticket in all three.

grammar.title: Един, една, едно
grammar.text: “One” follows the gender of the noun: един билет, една бира, едно кафе.

pronunciation.title: e-DEEN bee-LET
pronunciation.text: Both words are stressed on the end: е-DIN bi-LET.

target: Този автобус ходи ли до центъра?

translations.en-GB: Does this bus go to the centre?

mnemonic.title: Ходи: it walks
mnemonic.text: A Bulgarian bus «ходи», walks, to the centre: the same verb as for people.

grammar.title: До + “the”
grammar.text: «До» (to, as far as) takes the noun with “the”: центъра, the centre, from «център».

pronunciation.title: The ъ vowel
pronunciation.respelling: TO-zee af-to-BOOS HO-dee lee do TSEN-tuh-ruh
pronunciation.text: «Ъ» is a short, neutral vowel, like the a in “about”.

mnemonic.title: Спирам, спирка
mnemonic.text: «Спрете» (stop) and «спирка» (a stop) share a root: the bus stops at the stop.

grammar.title: Polite commands
grammar.text: «Спрете» is the polite command; to a friend you'd say «спри».

pronunciation.title: Тук, a short u
pronunciation.text: «Тук» is short, like “took”; «спре» starts with three consonants.

mnemonic.title: Струва: costs, is worth
mnemonic.text: «Струва» is both “costs” and “is worth”: «Струва си» means “it’s worth it”.

grammar.title: «Това» for what you point at
grammar.text: «Това» is “this” for anything you point at, whatever its gender.

pronunciation.title: to-VA
pronunciation.text: The stress in «това» falls on the last syllable.

mnemonic.title: Домати: tomatoes
mnemonic.text: «Домат» is the tomato, with a d where English has a t.

grammar.title: Masculine «един»
grammar.text: «Килограм» is masculine, so “one” is «един»; there is no “of”: «килограм домати».

pronunciation.title: Dark л
pronunciation.text: The л in «килограм» is a dark l, as in English “full”.

mnemonic.title: Торба: a bag
mnemonic.text: «Торбичка» is a little «торба» (bag): -ичка makes things small, like -ie in English.

grammar.title: «Може ли» asks politely
grammar.text: «Може ли» + a thing asks for it politely, like “Could I have…?”.

pronunciation.title: ж as in “pleasure”
pronunciation.text: «ж» is the s in “pleasure”.

mnemonic.title: Карта: card
mnemonic.text: «Карта» is a card, the same word as in Spanish and Russian.

grammar.title: «Ще» for the future
grammar.text: «Ще» before the verb makes the future: «ще платя», “I will pay”.

pronunciation.title: щ is “sht”
pronunciation.text: «Щ» in Bulgarian is “sht”, as in “ashtray”.

mnemonic.title: Call yourself
mnemonic.text: «Как се казвате?» is literally “How do you call yourself?”.

grammar.title: Polite «-те»
grammar.text: «Казвате» ends in -те, the polite “you”; to a friend say «Как се казваш?».

pronunciation.title: KAZ-va-te
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «казвате».

mnemonic.title: «Се»: oneself
mnemonic.text: «Се» is “oneself”: «Казвам се Мария» is “I call myself Maria”.

grammar.title: «Се» after the verb
grammar.text: At the start of a sentence «се» comes after the verb: «Казвам се…», never «Се казвам…».

pronunciation.title: Soft а
pronunciation.text: The unstressed а in «казвам» sounds closer to “uh”.

mnemonic.title: Pleasant to me
mnemonic.text: «Приятно ми е» is “it is pleasant to me”.

grammar.title: Short «ми»
grammar.text: «Ми» is the short “to me”; here it comes before «е».

pronunciation.title: One breath
pronunciation.text: Say it as one word: pri-YAT-no-mi-e.

mnemonic.title: From + where
mnemonic.text: «Откъде» is «от» (from) + «къде» (where).

grammar.title: «Сте»: you are
grammar.text: «Сте» is “you are”, polite or plural; answer «Аз съм от…», “I am from…”.

pronunciation.title: ъ as in “but”
pronunciation.text: «Ъ» is the u in “but”, said short.

mnemonic.title: Маса: mesa
mnemonic.text: «Маса» is table, like Spanish «mesa», from Latin «mensa».

grammar.title: «Двама» for people
grammar.text: «Двама» counts two men or a mixed pair; two women are «две».

pronunciation.title: MA-sa
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «маса» and «двама».

mnemonic.title: Order inside
mnemonic.text: «Препоръчам» (recommend) has «поръчам» (to order) inside it.

grammar.title: «Ще» + polite «-те»
grammar.text: «Ще препоръчате» is “will you recommend”, the polite form.

pronunciation.title: kak-VO
pronunciation.text: The ъ in «препоръчате» is short, like the u in “but”.

mnemonic.title: Смятам: I count
mnemonic.text: «Сметка» (bill) comes from «смятам», to count.

grammar.title: “The” at the end
grammar.text: Bulgarian puts “the” on the end of the word: «сметка» → «сметката».

pronunciation.title: SMET-ka-ta
pronunciation.text: The stress stays on the first syllable when -та is added.

mnemonic.title: Вкус: taste
mnemonic.text: «Вкусно» comes from «вкус», taste.

grammar.title: «Беше»: it was
grammar.text: «Беше» is “it was”; for “it is” say «Много е вкусно».

pronunciation.title: в sounds like f
pronunciation.text: Before к, в sounds like f: «вкусно» is “fkusno”.

target: Could I have a flat white, please?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли едно флат уайт, моля?

mnemonic.title: Flat and white
mnemonic.text: Picture the name: a «flat white» is coffee with a smooth, “flat” top of milk, not a tall foam like a cappuccino, and the milk makes it pale, “white”.

grammar.title: «Could I have…?»
grammar.text: «Could I have…?» is the polite way to ask for something at a counter. Say «could» rather than «I want», which sounds blunt, and finish with «please».

pronunciation.title: W is not V
pronunciation.ipa: [kʊd aɪ həv ə ˌflæt ˈwaɪt pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: kood eye huv uh flat WYTE pleez
pronunciation.text: Round your lips for the w in «white»: it is a short «oo» that glides into «ite», not a v. Keep the z at the end of «please» voiced, with a buzz, not a plain s.

target: I'll have a tea to take away, please

translations.bg-BG: Ще взема един чай за вкъщи, моля
translations.ru-RU: Я возьму чай с собой, пожалуйста

mnemonic.title: Take it away
mnemonic.text: Say it literally: you «take» the cup «away» with you. The shop's question mirrors it: «Eat in or take away?» (Americans say «to go»).

grammar.title: «I'll have…» decides on the spot
grammar.text: «I'll» is «I will»: use it for a decision made right now, «I'll have a tea». It is the other everyday way to order, next to «Could I have…?». «To take away» says how you want it.

pronunciation.title: Link «take away»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪl əv ə ˈtiː tə ˌteɪk əˈweɪ pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: ile uv uh TEE tuh tay-kuh-WAY pleez
pronunciation.text: Run «take away» together as «tay-kuh-WAY»: the k slides onto the weak «a» that follows. «Have» shrinks to a quick «uv», and «a» and «to» to a quick «uh».

target: Just a bit of milk, please

mnemonic.title: A bit, like a computer bit
mnemonic.text: Think of a computer «bit», the tiniest piece of data: «a bit of milk» is the tiniest amount. Most Britons take milk in their tea, so this request comes up all the time.

grammar.title: «A bit of» + something uncountable
grammar.text: Use «a bit of» before a word for something you don't count: «a bit of milk», «a bit of sugar». For things you can count, say «a few»: «a few biscuits».

pronunciation.title: One syllable, linked words
pronunciation.respelling: just uh BIT uv MILK pleez
pronunciation.text: Say «milk» as one syllable: don't slip a vowel in between the l and the k. Link «bit of» as «bi-tuv»: the t slides onto the weak «of».

target: Can I pay by card, please?

translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да платя с карта, моля?

mnemonic.title: «By» means “with”
mnemonic.text: «By card» is simply “with a card”: the small word «by» does the job that a small word does in Bulgarian and an ending does in Russian. Learn «by card», «by phone», «by bus» as a set.

grammar.title: No «the» after «by»
grammar.text: After «by», a way of paying or travelling takes no article: «by card», «by phone», «by bus». For cash, say «in cash». «Can I…?» asks whether something is possible or allowed.

pronunciation.title: No r in «card»
pronunciation.respelling: kun eye PAY by KAHD pleez
pronunciation.text: In standard Southern British English the r in «card» is silent: say a long «aa» and finish with d, «kaad». Don't roll an r, and keep the final d voiced.

target: A pint of lager and a half of cider, please

translations.bg-BG: Една пинта лагер и половин пинта сайдер, моля
translations.ru-RU: Пинту лагера и полпинты сидра, пожалуйста

mnemonic.title: Big glass, small glass
mnemonic.text: Order by size: «a pint» is the full glass, 568 ml, a little more than half a litre, and «a half» is half of it, about 284 ml.

grammar.title: «A half» means half a pint
grammar.text: In a pub, «a half» on its own means half a pint, and «of» links the measure to the drink: «a pint of lager», «a half of cider». Say the measure first, then the drink.

pronunciation.title: Weak «of», silent l
pronunciation.ipa: [ə ˈpaɪnt əv ˈlɑːɡə ən ə ˈhɑːf əv ˈsaɪdə pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: uh PINT uv LAH-guh un uh HAHF uv SY-duh pleez
pronunciation.text: «Of» shrinks to a short «uv», not «off», and the l in «half» is silent: say «haaf» with a long vowel.

target: It's my round. What are you having?

translations.bg-BG: Този път черпя аз. Какво ще пиеш?
translations.ru-RU: Теперь моя очередь угощать. Что будешь пить?

mnemonic.title: A round, like in boxing
mnemonic.text: A «round» of drinks works like a round in boxing or a game: everyone takes a turn. When it is your turn to buy for the whole group, you say «It's my round».

grammar.title: «Having» for drinking
grammar.text: «Have» also means eat or drink, and in that meaning it takes «-ing» for the present moment: «What are you having?» asks what you want right now.

pronunciation.title: A soft r, and -ing without g
pronunciation.ipa: [ɪts maɪ ˈraʊnd ˈwɒt ə jə ˈhævɪŋ]
pronunciation.respelling: its my ROWND. WOT uh yuh HAV-ing
pronunciation.text: The English r is not rolled: curl the tongue back without touching anything. End «having» with the «ng» of «sing», not a hard g.

target: Two fish and chips, please. We're on table six

translations.bg-BG: Две порции фиш енд чипс, моля. Ние сме на маса шест
translations.ru-RU: Две порции фиш-энд-чипс, пожалуйста. Мы за шестым столиком

fish and chips.bg-BG: фиш енд чипс (риба с пържени картофи)

mnemonic.title: Chips are not crisps
mnemonic.text: Fish and chips come as one unit, hot and wrapped in paper. British «chips» are thick fried potatoes, not the thin ones from a bag: those are «crisps».

grammar.title: The number follows the noun
grammar.text: A table is named with its number after it: «table six», with no «the» and no «of». People often say «on» with a table number: «We're on table six».

pronunciation.title: Short i: fish, chips, six
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈtuː ˈfɪʃ ən ˈtʃɪps pliːz wɪər ɒn ˈteɪbl̩ ˈsɪks]
pronunciation.respelling: TOO FISH un CHIPS pleez. weer on TAY-bul SIKS
pronunciation.text: The vowel in «fish», «chips» and «six» is a short, relaxed «i», not the long «ee» of «sheep». Say it quickly and let the consonants finish the word.

target: Cheers, mate. I'll get the next one

translations.bg-BG: Мерси, приятел. Следващото е от мен

mnemonic.title: «Cheers» does two jobs
mnemonic.text: «Cheers» is the toast when glasses clink and also a casual “thanks” when someone hands you a drink. Keep both meanings in one word.

grammar.title: «One» replaces the noun
grammar.text: «One» stands in for a noun that is already understood: «the next one» means “the next drink” (or round). «I'll get» is the everyday offer to buy; «get» means buy here.

pronunciation.title: th in «the», silent r
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈtʃɪəz ˈmeɪt aɪl ˈɡet ðə ˈneks ˈwʌn]
pronunciation.respelling: CHEERZ MAYT ile GET thuh NEKS WUN
pronunciation.text: For «the», put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and buzz: it is «th», not z or d, followed by a quick «uh». The r in «cheers» is silent: say «chee-uz», ending on z.

target: A return ticket to Brighton, please

translations.bg-BG: Един билет за отиване и връщане до Брайтън, моля
translations.ru-RU: Билет туда и обратно до Брайтона, пожалуйста

mnemonic.title: Re-turn: turn back
mnemonic.text: «Return» is «re-» (back) plus «turn»: you turn back at the end of the trip. The opposite is a «single», one way only.

grammar.title: One noun describes another
grammar.text: A noun can describe another noun and stands in front of it, with no ending: «a return ticket». The destination follows «to»: «to Brighton».

pronunciation.title: Silent gh, stress on «-turn»
pronunciation.respelling: uh rih-TURN TIK-it tuh BRY-tn pleez
pronunciation.text: In «Brighton» the gh is silent: say «bry-tn», not «brig-hton». «Return» is stressed on its second syllable, «ri-TURN», with a long «er» vowel and no rolled r.

target: Excuse me, which platform is the train to London on?

translations.bg-BG: Извинете, от кой перон тръгва влакът за Лондон?
translations.ru-RU: Извините, с какой платформы отправляется поезд на Лондон?

mnemonic.title: Platform: a flat form
mnemonic.text: «Platform» comes from French «plate-forme», literally a “flat form” to stand on. Hear «plat» (flat) and «form» (shape) and picture the flat strip beside the track.

grammar.title: «Which» + noun, «on» at the end
grammar.text: «Which» + a noun asks you to pick from a small set: «which platform», «which bus». The little word «on» stays at the end of the question: «Which platform is it on?»

pronunciation.title: Stress PLAT-form, w in «which»
pronunciation.ipa: [ɪkˈskjuːz miː ˈwɪtʃ ˈplætfɔːm ɪz ðə ˈtreɪn tə ˈlʌndən ɒn]
pronunciation.respelling: ik-SKYOOZ mee, WICH PLAT-form iz thuh TRAYN tuh LUN-dun on
pronunciation.text: English stresses the first syllable, «PLAT-form», unlike the Bulgarian and Russian word for it. The «wh» in «which» is just w: round your lips and don't say v.

target: Does this bus go to the city centre?

translations.bg-BG: Този автобус отива ли в центъра?

mnemonic.title: Centre is a word you know
mnemonic.text: «Centre» is the same word as the Bulgarian and Russian one for “the middle”, spelled with «-re» in British English. Bus fronts in British cities often show «City Centre» as the destination.

grammar.title: «Does» + go, not goes
grammar.text: In a question with «does», the main verb has no -s: «Does this bus go…?», not «Does this bus goes…?». The -s already sits on «does».

pronunciation.title: A short «uh», voiced z
pronunciation.ipa: [dʌz ðɪs ˈbʌs ˈɡəʊ tə ðə ˌsɪti ˈsentə]
pronunciation.respelling: duz this BUS GOH tuh thuh sit-ee SEN-tuh
pronunciation.text: The vowel in «does» and «bus» is a short, relaxed «uh»: don't round it into an «o». «Does» ends in a buzzing z: keep it voiced, while «bus» ends in a plain s.

target: Where do I change for Victoria?

translations.bg-BG: Къде да се прехвърля за Виктория?
translations.ru-RU: Где мне пересесть, чтобы доехать до Виктории?

mnemonic.title: Change like clothes
mnemonic.text: You change trains the way you change clothes: take one off, put another on. «Change for Victoria» means “swap here to get to Victoria”.

grammar.title: Change for where you're going
grammar.text: «Change for» is followed by where you want to end up, not by where you swap: «Change for Victoria» means you swap trains to reach Victoria. A question with an ordinary verb such as «change» needs «do»: «Where do I change…?».

pronunciation.title: End of «change», stress in Victoria
pronunciation.respelling: WAIR duh eye CHAYNJ fuh vik-TOR-ee-uh
pronunciation.text: «Change» ends in a soft, voiced «j», as in «judge»: don't harden it to «ch». In «Victoria» the stress falls on «-tor-»: vik-TOR-ee-uh, and the v is a real v, with the teeth on the lip.

mnemonic.title: How + much
mnemonic.text: Two small words: «how» and «much», literally “how a lot?”. Say them together whenever you see a price tag.

grammar.title: Is for one, are for many
grammar.text: «How much» takes «is» for one thing or a mass («How much is the milk?») and «are» for several things («How much are the apples?»). Match the verb to what you're asking about.

pronunciation.title: Light h, «the» before a vowel
pronunciation.text: The h of «how» is a light puff of breath, much softer than the scraping «kh» of Bulgarian and Russian. Before a vowel «the» turns into «thee»: «thee APPLES».

target: Have you got a carrier bag, please?

mnemonic.title: A bag that carries
mnemonic.text: Hear «carry» inside «carrier»: a carrier bag is simply the bag that carries your shopping home. Say «carrier bag» as one chunk.

grammar.title: «Have you got…?»
grammar.text: «Have you got…?» is an everyday British question: «have» moves in front of «you», with no «do». «Do you have…?» is also correct and common.

pronunciation.title: Final v and g stay voiced
pronunciation.ipa: [hæv jə ˈɡɒt ə ˈkæriə ˌbæɡ pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: hav yuh GOT uh KA-ree-uh bag pleez
pronunciation.text: The v at the end of «have» and the g at the end of «bag» must keep their buzz: «bag» is not «back», and «have» is not «haf». Voice them, then stop.

target: Is there a corner shop near here?

mnemonic.title: Corner, like in football
mnemonic.text: «Corner» is the football word you already know, and a «corner shop» is the small shop on the corner of a street, often open late. Picture it glowing on the corner.

grammar.title: «Is there a…?»
grammar.text: «Is there a…?» asks whether one thing exists nearby. For several things say «Are there any…?»: «Are there any shops near here?».

pronunciation.title: Long «aw», short «o»
pronunciation.ipa: [ɪz ðeər ə ˈkɔːnə ˌʃɒp nɪə ˈhɪə]
pronunciation.respelling: iz thair-uh KAW-nuh shop neer HEER
pronunciation.text: Hold the vowel of «corner» long, «kaw», and keep the one in «shop» short. None of these words has a rolled r: «corner» ends in a soft «uh», and «near» and «here» glide to a soft «uh».

target: Excuse me, is this till open?

mnemonic.title: The till that dings
mnemonic.text: Picture the cash drawer that pops open with a ding at the end of the queue: that is the «till» (Americans say «register»).

grammar.title: «Excuse me», then the question
grammar.text: «Excuse me» opens the question and politely gets someone's attention. In «Is this till open?» the «is» comes first to make the question, with no «do».

pronunciation.title: Excuse ends in z
pronunciation.respelling: ik-SKYOOZ mee, iz this TIL OH-pun
pronunciation.text: The verb «excuse» ends in a buzzing z, «ik-SKYOOZ», with the stress on «-cuse». In «this», put the tip of your tongue between your teeth.

target: Hi, I'm Alex. Nice to meet you

translations.bg-BG: Здравей, аз съм Алекс. Приятно ми е

mnemonic.title: Nice = pleasant
mnemonic.text: Line the words up with your own language: «nice» is “pleasant”, «to meet you» is “to get to know you”. Bulgarian and Russian greet with “pleasant” too, so you can map it word for word.

grammar.title: English always needs «be»
grammar.text: Unlike Russian, English always uses the verb «be»: «I'm Alex» (I am Alex), never «I Alex». The short form «I'm» is what you hear in speech.

pronunciation.title: Long «ee» in «meet»
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈhaɪ aɪm ˈælɪks ˈnaɪs tə ˈmiːt juː]
pronunciation.respelling: HY ime AL-iks NYSS tuh MEET yoo
pronunciation.text: Hold the vowel of «meet»: it is a long «ee», much longer than the short vowel in «it». With a short vowel it would sound like «mit». The t then joins «you» smoothly.

mnemonic.title: The answer echoes «from»
mnemonic.text: Answer with the same word that ends the question: «Where are you from?» — «I'm from…». Hold on to «from» and you have both halves.

grammar.title: «From» stays at the end
grammar.text: In English the little word «from» goes at the end of the question: «Where are you from?», not «From where are you?», which sounds stiff. Keep «are you» in that order.

pronunciation.title: Linking r
pronunciation.text: The r in «where» is silent on its own, but it comes back when a vowel follows: «where are» sounds like «WAIR-uh». Stress «from», the last word, and keep its vowel short and round.

target: It's a lovely day, isn't it?

mnemonic.title: A tail that asks for a nod
mnemonic.text: Stick «isn't it?» on the end of a remark like a little tail: it works like the small “right?” words of Bulgarian and Russian. People usually answer «It is» or «Lovely».

grammar.title: Tag questions
grammar.text: A tag question turns a remark into an invitation to agree. After a positive sentence with «is», add the negative: «It is… isn't it?». Match the verb: «They are… aren't they?».

pronunciation.title: Join the words
pronunciation.respelling: its uh LUV-lee DAY IZ-unt it
pronunciation.text: Run «it's a» together as «it-sa», with a quick «uh» for «a». «Isn't it» flows as «iz-nt-it», the t sliding onto «it». The z in «isn't» is voiced: it buzzes.

mnemonic.title: How is it going along?
mnemonic.text: The words are almost a picture: «how is it going along?». Bulgarian and Russian use their verb “to go” for the same question, so you already think this way.

grammar.title: A greeting more than a question
grammar.text: «How's it going?» is a greeting more than a real question: people answer «Not bad, thanks. You?» or «Good, thanks». «How's» is the short form of «how is».

pronunciation.title: A glide in «going»
pronunciation.text: The vowel in «going» glides from a relaxed «uh» to a hint of «oo»: it is never a pure «o». «How's it» joins up as «how-zit», with a voiced z.

mnemonic.title: Moloko: milk
mnemonic.text: «Молоко» is “milk”: the “moloko plus” milk bar in A Clockwork Orange borrowed the word from Russian. «Кофе» is the coffee you already know, so «кофе с молоком» is coffee with a splash of moloko.

grammar.title: «С» + instrumental
grammar.text: After «с» (“with”) the noun takes the instrumental case, so «молоко» becomes «молоком». English and Bulgarian leave the noun as it is; Russian changes its ending.

pronunciation.title: Weak vowels in молоком
pronunciation.text: Only the last syllable of «молоком» is stressed, so the first two о shrink to short, weak vowels: muh-luh-KOHM. Say «с молоком» as one smooth word, with «с» leaning on it.

translations.en-GB: A tea without sugar, if that's all right

mnemonic.title: Сахар: saccharin
mnemonic.text: «Чай» is the “chai” of chai latte. «Сахар» (sugar) is a distant relative of “saccharin”, so picture a sweetener packet and say «без сахара»: without it.

grammar.title: «Без» + genitive
grammar.text: «Без» (“without”) is followed by the genitive case: «сахар» becomes «сахара». Many masculine nouns end in -а in the genitive. «Если можно» (“if it is possible”) softens a request.

pronunciation.title: Fading vowels in сахара
pronunciation.text: In «сахара» only the first а is stressed, and the last two vowels fade to a short “uh”: SAH-khuh-ruh. The х is a rasp from the back of the throat, like “loch”, not a k.

translations.en-GB: I'll have a cappuccino to take away

mnemonic.title: С собой: with yourself
mnemonic.text: «С собой» is literally “with oneself”: picture yourself walking out with the cup in your hand. «Капучино» is the Italian word you already know, and «возьму» means “I'll take”.

grammar.title: «Возьму»: I'll take
grammar.text: «Возьму» looks like a present tense, but it is the future of one completed act: “I will take it”. It is the natural way to say what you are going to have, and Russian needs no word for “will” here.

pronunciation.title: Stress on -МУ and -ЧИ-
pronunciation.text: The stress is on the last syllable of «возьму» and on «чи» in «капучино»; the unstressed vowels around them stay short. The soft sign in «возьму» softens the з, so do not add a vowel after it: vuz-MOO.

translations.en-GB: Could I have the bill, please?

mnemonic.title: При-нести: carry it over
mnemonic.text: «Принесите» is «при-» (towards) plus «нести» (to carry): “carry it over to me”. «Счёт» belongs with «считать», “to count”: the bill is what the waiter has counted up.

grammar.title: Polite imperative: -те
grammar.text: «Принесите» is the polite “bring”: it is the friendly «Принеси» plus -те. The same form speaks to a group; to one friend or a child you say plain «Принеси».

pronunciation.title: сч is a long soft щ
pronunciation.text: «Сч» in «счёт» is read as one long, soft “sh” (the same sound as «щ»), softer and longer than the “sh” in “sheep”: SHCHYOT. The stress is on -СИ- in «принесите».

mnemonic.title: Метро: stress the end
mnemonic.text: «Метро» is the word you know, only with the stress on the end: myih-TRO. «Где здесь…?» is literally “where here…?”, so you can finish it with any place: «Где здесь аптека?».

grammar.title: No “is” in the present
grammar.text: Russian leaves out the present tense of “to be”: «Где здесь метро?» is literally “Where here metro?”, with no “is”.

pronunciation.title: гд and the weak е
pronunciation.text: «Гд» in «где» is two consonants together, g and d, with no vowel between them: gdyeh. In «метро» the unstressed е sounds like a short “ih”: myih-TRO.

mnemonic.title: Билет: billet-doux
mnemonic.text: «Билет» goes back to the French «billet», a short note (as in the English “billet-doux”): a ticket is a little note that lets you through the gate.

grammar.title: «Один» agrees with the noun
grammar.text: «Один» changes with the gender of the noun: «один билет» (masculine), «одна карта» (feminine), «одно место» (neuter). «Билет» is masculine, so it takes «один».

pronunciation.title: Stress on the last syllable
pronunciation.text: «Один», «билет» and «метро» are all stressed on their last syllable: uh-DYEEN, byih-LYET, myih-TRO. The л in «билет» is soft, almost “ly”.

translations.en-GB: Does this bus go to the centre?
translations.bg-BG: Този автобус отива ли до центъра?

mnemonic.title: Words you already know
mnemonic.text: «Автобус» is “auto-bus” and «центр» is “centre”: you already know most of this question. Only «идёт», “goes”, is new: picture a bus with «ЦЕНТР» on its destination sign.

grammar.title: «Идёт»: a bus “goes”
grammar.text: A bus on a route is said to «идти» (literally “to walk”): «автобус идёт». After «до» (“as far as”) the noun takes the genitive: «центр» becomes «центра».

pronunciation.title: ц and the f in автобус
pronunciation.text: «Ц» is one sound, “ts”, as in “cats”: TSEN-truh. The в in «автобус» is said as “f” because т follows it: uhf-TOH-boos.

translations.en-GB: Which stop do I get off at?
translations.bg-BG: На коя спирка трябва да сляза?

выходить.en-GB: to get off, to go out

mnemonic.title: Выход: the exit sign
mnemonic.text: Every exit sign in Russia says «ВЫХОД»: it is «вы-» (out) plus «ход» (going). «Выходить» is the verb, “to go out”: you step out of the bus at your stop.

grammar.title: «Мне» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Мне» (“to me”) followed by an infinitive asks what you are supposed to do: «Мне выходить?» is “Should I get off?”. No word for “should” is needed; the question words «на какой остановке» simply go in front.

pronunciation.title: The sound ы
pronunciation.text: «Ы» (“uy” in the respelling) has no English or Bulgarian twin: say the “i” of “bit”, then pull the tongue back as if about to say “oo”, but keep the lips spread. It comes right after в in «выходить».

mnemonic.title: «Сколько»: a three-beat question
mnemonic.text: Say it as a drumbeat, SKOL-ko EH-tuh STOH-eet, one beat per word, while you point at the price. «Сколько» is “how much”, and «стоит» is “costs”, so the whole question is “how much this costs”.

grammar.title: «Стоит» or «стоят»
grammar.text: «Стоит» is “costs” for one thing; for several things use «стоят»: «Сколько стоят помидоры?». The question word comes first, and no helper verb like “does” is needed.

pronunciation.title: Soft ль and weak endings
pronunciation.text: The л in «сколько» is soft, close to “ly”, and the endings of «сколько» and «это» fade to a short “uh”: SKOL'-kuh EH-tuh. All three words are stressed on the first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Помидор: golden apple
mnemonic.text: «Помидор» comes from the Italian «pomodoro», “golden apple”: the same word as in “pomodoro” sauce. So «килограмм помидоров» is a kilo of golden apples.

grammar.title: Amounts take the genitive plural
grammar.text: After a measure such as «килограмм» the goods stand in the genitive plural, which is why «помидоры» becomes «помидоров». The Russian ending does the job of “of”.

pronunciation.title: Final в sounds like f
pronunciation.text: A voiced consonant at the end of a word is said as its voiceless twin, so the в in «помидоров» sounds like “f”: puh-myih-DOH-ruhf. The stress is on -ДО-.

mnemonic.title: Пакет and есть
mnemonic.text: «Пакет» is “packet”: in Russian it is also the carrier bag you get at a shop or stall. Hear «есть» as “yest”, a bit like “yes”: yes, there is some.

grammar.title: “Have” is «у … есть»
grammar.text: In everyday speech Russian does not use a verb “to have”: it says «У вас есть…?», literally “At you there is…?”. The thing you ask about stays in its basic form: «пакет».

pronunciation.title: Soft есть and softened к
pronunciation.text: «Есть» starts with a “ye” and ends in a soft “-st'”: say the т with the tongue flat and high, without a vowel after it. The к in «пакет» is also softened by the е: puh-KYET.

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да платя с карта?

mnemonic.title: Картой: by card
mnemonic.text: Picture tapping your card on the terminal: «карта» is the “card” of English (both go back to Latin «charta»). The verb «заплатить» is “to pay”, and the ending -ой in «картой» means “by card”.

grammar.title: Means: instrumental, no preposition
grammar.text: To say “by card” Russian uses the instrumental case alone: «картой», with no «с». Use «с» only for “together with” («с молоком»). Feminine nouns in -а usually take -ой.

pronunciation.title: Stress at the end, then at the start
pronunciation.text: «Заплатить» is stressed on its last syllable, but «картой» on its first: zuh-pluh-TEET', KAR-tuhy. The ending -ой in «картой» is unstressed and weak, not a full “oy”.

mnemonic.title: Literally “how do they call you”
mnemonic.text: «Как вас зовут?» is literally “How do they call you?”: «зовут» comes from «звать», “to call”, so picture people shouting your name across a square.

grammar.title: «Вас» (polite) or «тебя»
grammar.text: «Вас» is the polite (or plural) “you”, the accusative of «вы»; with a friend or a child say «Как тебя зовут?». The verb «зовут» is “they call”, so there is no “is” in the phrase.

pronunciation.title: Stress at the end
pronunciation.text: The stress falls on the last syllable, «зовут», so the first о shrinks to a short, weak vowel: zuh-VOOT. «Как вас» is said almost as one word, with «вас» light and quick.

mnemonic.title: Меня and тебя rhyme
mnemonic.text: «Меня» (“me”) and «тебя» (“you”) rhyme, so keep them as a pair: «Меня зовут…», «Как тебя зовут?». Put your own name in place of «Анна».

grammar.title: “I am called”: меня зовут
grammar.text: Russian does not say “my name is”: it says «Меня зовут Анна», literally “They call me Anna”. «Меня» is the accusative of «я», and the name stays in its basic form.

pronunciation.title: Soft н and long нн
pronunciation.text: In «меня» the н is soft, one “ny” sound, and the stress is on the last syllable: myih-NYA. The double нн in «Анна» is held a little longer: AN-nuh.

translations.bg-BG: Много ми е приятно да се запознаем

mnemonic.title: Приятно: a pleasant yacht
mnemonic.text: Hear «приятно» as “pree-YACHT-no” and picture a pleasant first meeting on a yacht. Inside «познакомиться» you can spot «знакомый», “familiar”: you become familiar with someone.

grammar.title: «Приятно» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Приятно» (“it is pleasant”) can be followed straight by an infinitive: «Приятно познакомиться» is “(It's) pleasant to meet”. There is no “I” and no “is”; «очень» makes it warmer.

pronunciation.title: -ться sounds like “tsa”
pronunciation.text: The ending -ться is said “tsuh”: «познакомиться» ends in “-myih-tsuh”, not “-tisya”. The stress is on -КО-: puh-znuh-KOH-myih-tsuh.

mnemonic.title: Откуда: from where
mnemonic.text: «Откуда» is «от» (“from”) plus «куда» (“where to”): the arrow leaves a place. «Родом» belongs with «родина» (“homeland”) and «родиться» (“to be born”): where were you born?

grammar.title: Three kinds of “where”
grammar.text: Russian splits “where” in three: «где» (being somewhere), «куда» (going somewhere) and «откуда» (coming from somewhere). This phrase asks about origin, so it is «откуда».

pronunciation.title: The tapped р
pronunciation.text: The р in «родом» is a quick tap or trill of the tongue tip behind the teeth, like the r in Spanish “pero”, not the English “r”. The stress is on -КУ- and РО-: uht-KOO-duh, RO-duhm.

mnemonic.title: Столик: a little stool-table
mnemonic.text: «Стол» is related to the English “stool”, and -ик makes it small: a «столик» is a little table, which is what you book in a restaurant.

grammar.title: «На двоих»: two people
grammar.text: «На двоих» is “for two people”. For people, Russian often uses the collective «двое», «трое» (here in the form «двоих», «троих») instead of the plain «два», «три».

pronunciation.title: дв and the weak о
pronunciation.text: «Дв» in «двоих» is two consonants, d and v, said together. The о before the stressed и shrinks to a weak “uh”: dvuh-EEKH. The final х is a rasp at the back of the throat, not a k.

mnemonic.title: Recommend, in Cyrillic
mnemonic.text: «Порекомендовать» hides the word “recommend”: по + рекомендовать. Read it syllable by syllable and you already have most of it.

grammar.title: «Мочь»: г becomes ж
grammar.text: «Вы можете» means “you can” and is followed by an infinitive. In «мочь» the г of «я могу» becomes ж in «ты можешь», «вы можете».

pronunciation.title: что is “shto”
pronunciation.text: «Что» is spelled with ч but said “shto”. The long word «порекомендовать» has one stress, on the last syllable, -ВАТЬ; every vowel before it is weak.

target: Я бы хотел рыбу и салат

translations.en-GB: I'd like the fish and a salad, please
translations.bg-BG: Бих искал риба и салата, моля

mnemonic.title: Рыба: think of ribs
mnemonic.text: Hear «рыба» as “RUY-ba” and picture the ribs of a fish. «Салат» is the “salad” you know, with the stress on the last syllable.

grammar.title: «Я бы хотел»: I would like
grammar.text: «Бы» plus the past form «хотел» makes the polite “I would like”. «Бы» never changes, but «хотел» shows who is speaking: a woman says «Я бы хотела».

pronunciation.title: Two ы and two stressed ends
pronunciation.respelling: ya buy khuh-TYEL RUY-boo ee suh-LAHT
pronunciation.text: «Ы» appears twice, in «бы» and «рыбу» (“uy” in the respelling): the “i” of “bit” with the tongue pulled back. Stress falls on the last syllable of «хотел» and «салат»: khuh-TYEL, suh-LAHT.

translations.en-GB: Everything was very tasty, thank you

mnemonic.title: Спасибо: God save you
mnemonic.text: «Спасибо» began as «спаси Бог», “God save (you)”, so thanking someone is wishing them well. «Вкусно» (“tasty”) is built on «вкус», “taste”.

grammar.title: «Было» agrees with «всё»
grammar.text: «Всё» (“everything”) is neuter, so the past tense is «было»; with a masculine subject it would be «был», with a feminine «была». «Вкусно» is an adverb here and does not change.

pronunciation.title: в sounds like f
pronunciation.text: Before voiceless sounds в is said as “f”: «всё» is FSYOH and «вкусно» is FKOOS-nuh. The ё in «всё» is stressed and sounds like “yo”.
